case_studies.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
case_studies.abstract: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.
case_studies.summary: The study tackles the problem of documentation lagging behind code changes, which harms LLM agents that rely on up‑to‑date docs. A triage agent called TriAgent was built to spot and fix gaps, reviewing 499 tickets over 43 days and finding 92 gaps with 81% accuracy. The system improved later answers by 71% when gaps were repaired, showing it can keep docs current for better AI support.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Run a TriAgent‑style bot that monitors support tickets and code‑doc mismatches; 2) Use the bot’s flagged gaps to prioritise documentation updates; 3) Validate updates with a quick human check before publishing to keep LLMs accurate.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a deployed multi‑agent system for detecting and repairing documentation gaps, directly affecting how IT engineers manage internal knowledge bases and support tickets. The system has been operational for 43 days, indicating a mature, tested solution with released code or at least a working prototype. Its applicability to real‑world documentation workflows and potential to be offered as a SaaS or internal tool within a short timeframe gives it high monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
case_studies.abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that a deep‑reinforcement‑learning controller can run on a real building’s heat‑pump and underfloor heating system, keeping temperature comfortable while cutting energy use. The researchers built a digital twin, trained a DRL agent offline, and then deployed it with no further tuning. This proves that data‑driven HVAC control is feasible in occupied homes, but the work is mainly relevant to building‑management software, not core cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage building‑management or IoT platforms for HVAC, check if your system can integrate a DRL model: 1) Create a digital twin of your building, 2) Train a DRL agent offline using simulated data, 3) Deploy the trained policy to your real control system without online fine‑tuning.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses DRL for building heating control, which is peripheral to core IT infrastructure concerns such as cloud services, endpoint management, or SaaS tooling. While it includes a real-world deployment, the domain is niche and unlikely to influence daily operations of IT engineers in the described environment. Monetisation potential is limited as the solution is specific to HVAC systems and would require significant integration effort. Therefore, scores are low across all criteria.
